_about: Ten real incidents (2021-2025) where the hard part was tracing a flaw to what you ship and who fixes it. Facts checked against the sources listed with each case on 2026-10-17. setup_db.py loads these as (:Case)-[:ABOUT]->(:Vulnerability); /api/cases replays each one against Fernwave's graph.

cases.name: Log4Shell
cases.happened: A Java logging library used almost everywhere ran code sent inside a log message. Attacks started about a week before the public disclosure.
cases.hard_part: Log4j sat inside thousands of other components. The US Cyber Safety Review Board called it an endemic vulnerability that could linger for a decade or more.

cases.name: libwebp image flaw
cases.happened: A flaw in Google's WebP image library was used in real attacks. It was first published as a Chrome issue, then widened to libwebp itself.
cases.hard_part: The library is bundled in browsers, Electron apps, 1Password for macOS and image libraries such as Pillow. Teams that only checked for Chrome missed it.

cases.name: HTTP/2 Rapid Reset
cases.happened: Opening and instantly cancelling HTTP/2 streams produced the largest DDoS attacks recorded at the time. Google's peak was more than 8× its previous record.
cases.hard_part: One protocol flaw, many separate fixes: Netty, Go, nginx and others each needed their own patch, so you had to know which one every service used.

cases.name: MOVEit Transfer
cases.happened: The Cl0p gang mass-exploited a file-transfer product and stole data from its customers, and from their customers.
cases.hard_part: British Airways, the BBC and Boots never ran MOVEit. Their payroll provider Zellis did. The exposure was in a supplier, not in their own code.

cases.name: Citrix Bleed
cases.happened: Remote-access gateways leaked session tokens, so attackers skipped passwords and MFA. LockBit used it against Boeing, ICBC's US arm and DP World Australia.
cases.hard_part: Installing the update didn't kick out attackers already holding stolen sessions. You also had to know to end every session: the 'how we fixed it' step.

cases.name: Ivanti Connect Secure
cases.happened: Two chained flaws in VPN gateways gave attackers unauthenticated control. CISA ordered federal agencies to disconnect the devices, and CISA itself lost two systems to the same flaws.
cases.hard_part: Mitigations, partial patches and full patches came weeks apart. Every device had to be tracked as patched, mitigated or still exposed.

cases.name: xz utils backdoor
cases.happened: An account called 'Jia Tan' became a maintainer of a small compression library and hid a backdoor in versions 5.6.0 and 5.6.1. An engineer found it by chance, from slow SSH logins.
cases.hard_part: Every company had to answer one question at once: do we ship xz 5.6.0 or 5.6.1 anywhere, even in a build image?

cases.name: Palo Alto PAN-OS
cases.happened: A firewall flaw let unauthenticated attackers run code as root. It was exploited before any fix existed, and attackers moved on into victims' networks.
cases.hard_part: Only some versions with two settings turned on were exposed. Knowing exactly which devices ran which version and configuration decided who was at risk.

cases.name: SharePoint ToolShell
cases.happened: Self-hosted SharePoint servers were hacked in bulk, including the US nuclear weapons agency (NNSA). The flaw got around an earlier patch.
cases.hard_part: Teams that had patched in early July were still exposed. They needed to know which servers had the second fix, not just 'a' fix.

cases.name: React2Shell
cases.stat_label: from disclosure to CISA's exploited list
cases.happened: A maximum-severity flaw in React Server Components let anyone run code on web servers. A default Next.js app was exploitable with no code changes.
cases.hard_part: Few teams chose React Server Components directly. They inherited them through Next.js and other frameworks.
